title: Year one close: the big lookout
hookLine: ahead: the Buddha's words in order, the great stories and teachers, the schools, the sources

lines: DAY ONE: ONE WORD, ONE BREATH.
A LEDGE THAT LOOKS BOTH WAYS.
cards: Three hundred thirty-one days ago, this path began with one word, metta, and one breath. Today is the last day of year one. On a trail, a lookout isn't the summit.

It's a ledge with a railing and maybe a bench, where the view opens both ways at once: the climb behind, and in front, ridge after ridge, blue and far away, more mountains than the map seemed to promise.
Yesterday was for the view back. Today is one glance back, and then a long look ahead.

teach.h: ONE GLANCE BACK AT FIVE CAMPS.
teach.b: The glance back, and only a glance, since yesterday took the long view: five camps, from first words through the stories, the practices and the Dhammapada to the depths. Now turn around.
In the Connected Discourses, the Buddha is staying in a grove of simsapa trees.

teach.h: A HANDFUL OF LEAVES, A WHOLE FOREST.
teach.b: He picks up a few leaves and asks the monks: which are more, the leaves in my hand, or the leaves in the forest? The forest, of course, they say. Just so, he tells them.
What he has come to know is like the forest. What he has taught is like the handful. Why only a handful?
Because the handful is what helps: suffering, its cause, its ending, and the way to its ending. So both are true at once. There's always more, and the handful is enough to walk with.
Here's the forest ahead. Year two is the Buddha's own words: the four truths and the eightfold path in depth, then the discourses read in order.
Year three is the great story and the teachers: the Buddha's life as a poem, the first disciples and their songs, and the teaching's long journey across Asia.

Year four is the schools, each in its own terms and never ranked: Theravada thought, the Mahayana sutras, Zen, Pure Land, the Tibetan traditions. Year five is the sources, a little Pali, and a life of practice.

teach.h: WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH DILIGENCE.
teach.b: In Rhys Davids's translation of the Buddha's last words: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!"
Everything made will change, this year included. Keep going, and keep going carefully.

how: Many Buddhists mark the end of a year or a retreat by resting in quiet sitting, recalling the teachings they have received, and renewing the three refuges before setting out again.

o: a final blessing given at a death
the calm that comes once striving stops
heedfulness: care that never slacks off

games.q: match each stretch of the hill to what it held.

s: the Buddha said he had taught everything he knew
in the simsapa grove he said what he taught was a handful; what he knew was a forest.
he taught the handful because it helps end suffering
suffering, its cause, its ending and the way: that's what was in his hand.
year four ranks the Buddhist schools from best to worst
each school is explained in its own terms, never ranked.

games.q: you're a monk in the simsapa grove. the Buddha holds up a few leaves and asks: which are more, these in my hand or those in the forest? what do you say?
games.why: the forest, the monks said, and he agreed: what he knew was the forest, what he taught was the handful, because the handful is what helps.

practice: Sit comfortably, breathe, and let your eyes find the farthest thing you can see, a window, the sky, a wall across the room: that is your lookout.

Let the year drift past like a landscape: a face, a story, a verse, a hard day you sat through anyway, none of it held on to. Then let your eyes soften and rest, with nothing to fix and nothing to finish.
If you take refuge, you can say the three refuges silently, once.

wordCard.voice: Appamada. Heedfulness, diligence, never slacking off: the word in the Buddha's last words, and the spirit of this lookout day.

orig.note: Pali appamāda: heedfulness, diligence, never slacking off; it's in the Buddha's last words.

carryVoice: Your line: there's always more. A handful of leaves comes with you into year two. Year one, done.

sources.ref: SN 56.31 (Simsapa Sutta, the handful of leaves)
DN 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta) VI.10, the last words
sources.q: Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!
